How does it feel to play a 44-minute
N.B.A.
game? Pretty much the same way it feels to play a regular 48-minute game, it turns out.
Before the preseason game between
the Nets
and the
Boston Celtics
on Sunday afternoon at Barclays Center, the Nets’ game host, Ally Love, explained to the crowd over the public address system that each quarter of the game would be abbreviated to 11 minutes from 12.
Last week, the N.B.A. announced that it would use the afternoon game to conduct a one-time experiment with a shorter format — a fanciful adjustment that, in the unlikely chance it were implemented, would ostensibly make the games more television-friendly and marginally lighten the wear and tear on players.
“So enjoy,” Love said, “as you’ll be witnessing some N.B.A. history.”
The writing of history, in this instance, turned out wholly unremarkable and, according to the players involved, barely perceptible in real time. After the game, people were at a loss for interesting things to say about it.
“Honestly, I forgot all about it,” Joe Johnson said in the locker room.
Andrei Kirilenko was asked what was different about the game, compared with a 48-minute contest. “Nothing,” he said with a blank stare.
Certain things did feel slightly off. It was just a bit strange, for example, to see 11 minutes on the clock at the start of every quarter. And both teams’ coaches said the pacing of the mandatory timeouts — which were reduced in the second and fourth quarters to two from three — was different from what they had long become accustomed to.
“That was the only time it seemed like it was quick,” said Nets Coach Lionel Hollins, who was more concerned about how poorly his team had rebounded in its 95-90 loss.
The time of the game, according to the official scorer’s report, was 1 hour 58 minutes. The average N.B.A. game without overtime in the 2013-14 regular season lasted 2:15, a league spokesman said.
Games in pro football, hockey and baseball averaged longer times in their previous full seasons, according to the Elias Sports Bureau. Unlike those leagues, the N.B.A. has never felt it imperative to shorten its games for viewers. Players around the league said in the days after the announcement that reducing the number of games would be a far more effective way of preserving their bodies.
The experiment, then, was relatively easy to shrug off. “It’s cool,” Deron Williams said after the announcement last week. “We can be the guinea pigs. It doesn’t bother me.”
Data from the game will be only vaguely useful, though, given that it was an exhibition game and both teams used their personnel differently from how they would in the regular season.
The intermission was shortened a minute as well, to 14 — still plenty of time for a group of children to play a spirited game of musical chairs at center court. And even with the reduction of two timeouts, there were a sufficient number of long stoppages to put on the normal dance team performances and T-shirt giveaways.
In all regards, it felt like a normal game until the fourth quarter, when both coaches called on their reserves to play out the final minutes.
And as the sloppy action lurched on, the game felt interminable in ways that had nothing to do with time, in ways that no rule tweak could have improved.

Throughout the Times headquarters on Eighth Avenue, the walls are decorated with news images from the past. In this series we’ll take you inside the building to see the photographs — many of them rich in history — and the stories behind them.
In December 2006, Todd Heisler photographed his first assignment for The Times:
experimental brain surgery
. The dramatic photo hangs on a wall across from Science editors’ desks on the second floor.
Todd Heisler on the photo:
Dec. 12, 2006. I had just joined the photography staff at The New York Times and my first assignment was a long, arduous day as the Science reporter Denise Grady and I followed Chris Ratuszny, then 26, as he underwent an experimental procedure to bypass an aneurysm the size of a golf ball that was rapidly growing behind his eye. After he was given anesthesia, electrodes were put into his scalp and pins were drilled into his skull to hold it steady for surgery.
That morning he would become the first person in the United States to have such a surgery using an excimer laser. The Dutch neurosurgeon who devised the laser procedure, Dr. Cornelius Tulleken, flew in from the Netherlands to help. Dr. David Langer, a brain surgeon at Roosevelt Hospital in Manhattan who led the operation. He was granted onetime approval from the Food and Drug Administration to perform the surgery, which had not yet been allowed in the United States.
They agreed to let us witness the surgery in its entirety, regardless of the outcome. As Dr. Langer said, this surgery would be risky in even the best of hands. Yet to watch the focus and stamina of the surgical team, who worked for more than nine hours, one might not have noticed it outright. The weight of what was transpiring was still palpable. I remember vividly watching Dr. Langer at the end of the procedure, waiting for his patient to awake in the O.R. As Denise Grady wrote: “He rested on a stool, leaning against the wall, his head bowed. He seemed unaware that he was bouncing his foot in time with a beeping monitor, matching Mr. Ratuszny’s every heartbeat.”
Shortly after, Mr. Ratuszny woke up. The surgery was a success. It was a relief to watch as Dr. Langer broke the good news to his parents and sister, who shed tears of joy and embraced in a hospital corridor.

Purveying a strangely sweet vulgarity, the romantic comedy
“Sex Ed”
commiserates with Eddie (
Haley Joel Osment
), 23, a would-be geometry teacher who’s as much a virgin in the bedroom as in the classroom. Everyone except Eddie, it seems, is getting some love, from the customers in the bagel shop where he works to his cheerfully randy roommate (a bang-on Glen Powell). So when he’s hired to supervise middle school detention, it seems particularly cruel that the one subject his students most need to learn is the one he may be least qualified to teach.
Playing straight guy to a sturdy supporting cast — especially Retta (
“Parks and Recreation”
) as a wise confidante and Matt Walsh (
“Veep”
) as a washed-up supervisor — Mr. Osment, with his baby face and cushiony body, retains a childlike air that softens the raunch. Navigating Bill Kennedy’s uninspired and only mildly amusing script (structured around an energetic endorsement for sex education in schools), he doesn’t so much drive the action as bounce from one humiliation to another. Filthy conversations abound, mostly with a handful of trash-talking students and a series of female characters apparently conjured from a frat-boy wish list.
Unevenly directed by Isaac Feder,
“Sex Ed”
droops. If you come for Retta’s “I got this” swagger, then stay for the improvised conversation between Mr. Walsh and Mr. Osment during the closing credits. It’s the freshest and funniest part of the movie.

Michael Powell at his desk on the third floor of the newsroom.
For two years,
Michael Powell
has written the
Gotham
column about New York politics and government. In July he will become a Sports of The Times columnist. Before he immerses himself in the world of sports, we asked him to reflect on his time writing about New York and New Yorkers.
I grew up in the prewar canyons of the Upper West Side of Manhattan. Each day as my best friend and I wended our way back from junior high and high school, we would stop by the 91st Street soda stand and pick up the tabloids and read as we walked, engorging ourselves on Pete Hamill, Murray Kempton, Jimmy Breslin and even Jose Torres, the light-heavyweight middleweight boxing champ who had become – in my memory anyway – a pretty damn good columnist.
Then there were the sports pages, with a no less wonderful cacophony of voices.
Later I discovered The Village Voice, Ellen Willis, Jack Newfield, Alexander Cockburn, Nat Hentoff, Wayne Barrett and so on, voices gloriously, intensely New York. This was column writing as if written in a congenitally contentious bleacher.
Still later I had the chance to work alongside Breslin, Kempton and the next generation, Jim Dwyer and Gail Collins.
Anyway, two  years ago, I was offered the chance to step into the line of march with this crowd, to hustle along and try not to embarrass myself. It was too delicious an opportunity to ignore.
I grew up in a rent-controlled apartment. I drove a cab and worked as a doorman, which was a useful introduction to this upstairs/downstairs city. And I worked for several years as a community organizer in the West Indian and Haitian neighborhood of East Flatbush.
My intent, as a columnist, was to seek out the city I knew and, more interesting, the continually changing city I half-knew. I found an intoxicating, change-in-a-blink-of-the-eye place. To wander Roosevelt Avenue in Jackson Heights and Elmhurst and interview transvestite prostitutes from Ecuador and find a fascinating Colombian who had opened a wonderful jazz club, Terraza 7, and mothers who worked 15 hours in restaurants for $5 an hour was to see a new New York given flesh and bone.
I recall wandering the vertical streets of University Heights in the Bronx and talking to residents. I found few who knew who was running for mayor, much less whom they would vote for.
Many were too caught up in the game of survival to pay attention yet to electoral politics. But this spoke as well to the self-defeating inanity of campaign consultants and the smart crowd, who long ago decided that the easier and more predictable way to win elections was to shrink rather than expand the pool of voters.
It is easier to pull out those ever-diminishing number of voters whom you know than risk engaging a world of those you don’t. So we’re left with a cramped, attenuated politics that dishonors the city. But whatever; that’s a column for another day.
Writing a city column can be wonderfully destructive of certainty. Often I thought I had decoded an issue, a character, and then I stumbled out and talked to New Yorkers and they confounded my thinking. Nearly two years back, we saw a horrific series of summer shootings, of the sort that once defined and scarred this city.
A young, soulful-eyed college student, Matt Shaw, back in East Harlem for the summer, was mistaken for someone else and shot down by a neighborhood gunslinger. In the Bronx, Kemar, a sweet 14-year-old kid, who had arrived the year before from the West Indies, was running home through thunder and rain after playing tennis. A random bullet fired by a random fool struck him in the head and so he died.
On a sun-filled day in early September 2012, I spent time with Paula Shaw-Leary, who was the mother of Matt. Then I journeyed to the Bronx to talk with Cassell Brooks, the father of Kemar.
Their anguish was elemental.
Our conversation turned to all these gangbangers and their guns. I had written a lot that year about the stop-and-frisk controversy, and I had come across and written of so many examples of innocent young men stopped and police excess.
These parents would hear nothing of that. They had ordered their sons to stay off the streets, worried that something would happen when they walked to the grocery store or went out with friends. These parents applauded those cops who cast a hawk’s eye on their blocks.
In wintertime, Ms. Shaw-Leary told me, she patted her sons’ coats. Her children called her Sergeant Strict, and she embraced that name. “I like
stop-and-frisk
,” she told me. “I stop and frisk my own kids! I tell Matt: ‘If a police officer stops you, don’t get macho. They are doing their jobs.’ ”
If the cops could find more of those illegal guns, their sons, these parents argued, might be alive.
I’m a father of two boys becoming young men, and these conversations sent me spinning into a morally grayer and more complex corner of that stop-and-frisk argument than I’d occupied before.
There is, too, the great pleasure of hearing from readers. Praise is always nice, and no doubt too addictive. More challenging and probably most useful are the emails and calls from readers who force you to reconsider, to let the second and third thoughts gain entry to your brain pan. I recently used the words
“Bull Connor” in an article
about the reaction of the Los Angeles Clippers to the racist remarks of the owner of the team, Donald Sterling. It was a turn of a phrase, a mention of a long-ago and brutish Southern sheriff. I thought it was clever.
A reader who has worked in the civil rights movement reminded me that such words come freighted with historical resonance. He argued that to use the term in relation to Sterling was a misappropriation of history, or at least an overreach. We had a cordial exchange of emails, more an exercise in understanding each other’s thinking than in trying to convince each other.
I confess that after thinking about it, I knew he was right. He’d given me the blessing of a second thought.
Anyway, I’m off into the new and complex world of sport. New York City remains woven into my DNA, and not just because I live in Flatbush and carry my tribal and hapless allegiances to the Mets, the Jets and the Knicks. I still want to see how some of these themes that preoccupy me — of poverty and inequity, of businessmen shaking down cities for subsidies and of the human experience — play out in the sports arena.
And I’m quite certain that readers will do their utmost to hold my feet to the fire.

Technology companies have taken over your stereo, television and home movies. Now they’re coming for your board games.
Google
announced Tuesday
that is had added about a dozen game applications, including sped-up versions of Scrabble and Monopoly, to its Chromecast streaming device. The idea is to turn living room TVs into a game board that friends and families could play in tandem, using their mobile phones as a joystick.
“This is our first attempt to rethink how a game can work with this new cast model,” said Rishi Chandra, director of product management for Chromecast.
The Chromecast is a small piece of hardware – a “dongle” in techspeak – that looks like the thumb drives people plug into their computers to save data. Instead of a computer, however, it plugs into most high-definition televisions as a means of connecting them to the Internet. Once it is plugged in, people can stream content from their mobile phones and tablets onto their televisions.
If this sounds familiar, that’s because there are a lot of streaming devices on the market, such as Apple TV, the
Roku streaming stick
and Amazon’s forthcoming
Fire TV Stick
. Have you ever crowded around a friend’s phone to watch a YouTube video or passed your phone around the living room to show off a picture of your darling nieces? These devices are supposed to fix those inconveniences by projecting a small screen onto a bigger screen.
People watch a lot of video on their phones and tablets. The idea of the Chromecast is to bring those videos onto a TV. The device works with a growing universe of movie and music apps like Netflix, HBO Go, Hulu Plus and Pandora.
Will games be a new front? If so, Google is starting small. Tuesday’s announcement includes about a dozen game apps. They include Scrabble Blitz and Monopoly Dash – leaner, faster versions of the board game classics – as well as less-well-known fare like a Google trivia game called Big Web Quiz.
The thing that makes this unique is that, to play these games via the Chromecast, users will use both their phones and their TVs.
Say that you and a friend wanted to play Scrabble Blitz, a timed game where people compete head-to-head to spell as many words as possible from a handful of letters. First you would have to both download the Scrabble Blitz app to your phones. Once you did that and connected to the Chromecast, you would spell the words on your respective smart phones, and they would show up on the TV.
“Once you have this connection between your phone and your TV, you can start to think about things that weren’t possible before,” said Mr. Chandra. Such as: “Can we build a new gaming experience around social games?”
Board games, for all their mid-century charm, are no strangers to modernization. Mark Blecher, a senior vice president at Hasbro whose responsibilities include digital gaming, ticked off various places where people can play Scrabble. You can play on the web. You can play on a mobile phone. You can play on a video game console, such as Microsoft’s Xbox. There are Scrabble lottery tickets and Scrabble slot machines.
Even the Scrabble board game has embraced technology: In addition to the no frills classic, there is a Scrabble Deluxe Edition, which has a rotating board. The company also sells a hand-held scorekeeper for people who are too lazy to add or multiply.
At least for now, you can’t play classic Scrabble through the Chromecast. The longer the game, the more it will drain a mobile phone’s precious battery. Also, when people play games on their phones, they are usually quick games like a round of Angry Birds.
“We know that most people on phones like to play things 3 minutes at a time, and the regular game isn’t a three minute experience,” said Mr. Blecher.
He added: “We’ll see how these games perform and there’s always an opportunity to do more things in the future.”
Beyond inserting itself into your living room, the Chromecast is a way for Google to add fuel to its fast-growing Play Store, an online store where people can buy mobile applications and content like movies. In its third-quarter earnings, Google reported that “other revenue,” a large portion of which is Google’s Play Store, increased 50 percent from the same quarter of last year, to $1.8 billion.

In Joseph Heller’s anti-war satire, “Catch 22,” the hero, Yossarian, is assigned to a censorship detail. He amuses himself by deleting all the adverbs and adjectives from soldiers’ letters, then all the articles, then everything but the articles, and so on. His job was to delete details that threatened operational security. The result was gibberish.
It seems the Central Intelligence Agency was inspired by Yossarian’s example.
The C.I.A. was given the task of censoring the Senate Intelligence Committee’s report denouncing none other than the C.I.A. for torturing prisoners, lying to its overseers in Congress about the torture, and exaggerating how much valuable information the torture provided (if any). The result was predictable and proof, if anyone still needed it, that having the subject of the report censor that report is a very bad idea.
When the White House approved the C.I.A.’s censorship (the term of art in Washington is “redaction”) and sent the report to the Hill, James Clapper, the Director of National Intelligence, said in his usual sneering way that 85 percent of the report was intact and that half the blackouts were made to footnotes.
The issue, of course, is not merely how much is deleted, but what is deleted. On Monday, McClatchy
reported
that C.I.A. censors had blacked out the pseudonyms used to protect the identities of agents involved in the detention and interrogation of suspected terrorists. That, McClatchy said, rendered parts of the report unintelligible.
“Redactions are supposed to remove names or anything that could compromise sources and methods, not to undermine the source material so that it is impossible to understand,” said Senator Martin Heinrich, the New Mexico Democrat, who is a member of the intelligence committee. “Try reading a novel with 15 percent of the words blacked out.”
Senator Dianne Feinstein, the committee chairwoman who ordered up the staff report, said the deletions eliminate or obscure “key facts” that underpin the report’s main conclusions. She said she would fight to have more of the report declassified and is meanwhile withholding it from publication.
Mark Mazetti
reported
in The Times today that Senator Carl Levin, Democrat of Michigan and chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, called the deletions “totally unacceptable.” They apparently included information that had been in the 2009 report on interrogation already published by Mr. Levin’s committee. The Senate committee and the C.I.A. are also at odds over the deletion of other intelligence information that was not obtained from interrogations but was important to the hunt for al Qaeda terrorists.
Asked about the dispute, the White House press secretary Josh Earnest, offered the usual boilerplate about national security reviews. Here’s how Yossarian might have quoted him: “It is BLANK that a BLANK process be carried out that BLANKS sources and BLANK and other BLANK that is BLANK to our BLANK BLANK.”

PARIS –The sculptor
Anish Kapoor
will be the next contemporary artist to be given a one-man show at the Château de Versailles. Mr. Kapoor’s show will run from June to October next year, the palace’s chief administrator, Catherine Pégard, said in an interview.
“It’s not easy to choose an artist for Versailles,” Ms. Pégard said. “It’s not a museum, or a gallery or an exhibition space.” She said that Mr. Kapoor, 60, had been chosen “because he has something particular to say in this setting.” The series of solo shows
began in 2008 with Jeff Koons
and has included Takashi Murakami among others.
Certainly Mr. Kapoor, who was born in India and has lived in London for decades, is no stranger to grandeur. He is probably best known recently for his “ArcelorMittal Orbit” in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in London, a convoluted cross between the Eiffel Tower and a Salvador Dalí surrealist fantasy that stands more than 375 feet high and is Britain’s tallest sculpture.
Nor is he a stranger to the Paris art scene: In 2011 he was the chosen artist for the annual Monumenta show, where his  “Leviathan,” a huge maroon balloon-like structure almost entirely filled the inside of the Grand Palais. “Leviathan” attracted more visitors during its six-week stint that any other Monumenta show,  a record presumably not lost on the Versailles selectors. Versailles itself packs in some 5 million visitors a year, with numbers peaking during the summer, when the contemporary art exhibition is a magnet for foreign tourists. Big crowds should mean big revenue — much needed when austerity is slicing into the government’s culture budget.

TORONTO — A year ago, when the
Yankees
opened their season in the Bronx against the Boston Red Sox, there was a noticeable void. It was felt during the pregame introductions when players like Kevin Youkilis and Travis Hafner were announced over the public-address system, but
Derek Jeter
was not.
It was felt again when the Yankees took the field and the player who ran to shortstop was Eduardo Nunez, not Jeter. In fact, Jeter missed all but 17 games last season as he experienced the most maddening, injury-marred season of his career.
But on Monday, Jeter — healthy and eager — is scheduled to be a part of all the festivities as the Yankees celebrate their 112th home opener, and Jeter’s last.
“We all look forward to the home opener,” Jeter said Sunday before the Yankees beat the
Toronto Blue Jays
, 6-4. “It almost doesn’t seem like the season is underway until you get your home opener. Especially missing last year, I’m looking forward to this one.”
The home fans are too, because this will be their first chance to shower him with their appreciation since he announced Feb. 12 that he will retire after this, his 20th season with the Yankees. Jeter has already been celebrated by the fans in Houston and Toronto during each of his at-bats, but Monday is destined to involve several lengthy, heartfelt standing ovations for the 39-year-old Yankees captain.
Jeter will enter Monday afternoon’s game against the Baltimore Orioles in style. With two hits Sunday, he moved past Paul Molitor into eighth place on the career hits list with 3,320, the fourth most in the American League. He is 99 hits from tying Carl Yastrzemski for seventh.
“It feels good,” Jeter said. “I’d be lying if I said otherwise. It’s an accomplishment. You’ve got to play for a long time to be close to something like this. I just try to play; try to be consistent. I want to be out there every day. If you do it long enough, then some of these things are attainable.
“It’s definitely special. But I’m not going to go home and celebrate, because we have a game tomorrow. But it’s something I take a lot of pride in.”
Jeter’s two hits raised his batting average to .250, and the Yankees collected nine hits altogether. One of those was their first home run, a line drive to right field by Brett Gardner in the fourth inning, as the Yankees held on to win their first series of the season. After dropping the first two games in Houston, the Yankees come home for the first time feeling a little better about themselves.
Manager Joe Girardi said that after the team’s slow start, having a 3-3 record felt somehow better than a .500 mark.
The Yankees scored three times in the first inning, but
C. C. Sabathia
gave up a leadoff home run to Melky Cabrera, who homered in each of the three games in the series. Sabathia, in his 400th start, settled down and held on to earn his first win of the season. In the sixth, he gave up four straight hits and three runs but got out of the inning. The victory was his seventh in eight decisions at Rogers Centre.
Sabathia was charged with four runs and seven hits in six innings, but walked off the mound leading, 6-4. Three relievers made it stand up. Adam Warren and Shawn Kelley each threw a scoreless inning, and David Robertson earned his second save.

The festivities Monday will feature a tribute to the so-called Core Four members of the Yankees’ five World Series teams from 1996 to 2009. Andy Pettitte and Mariano Rivera will throw tandem ceremonial first pitches to Jorge Posada and Jeter, the last member of the group still playing.
“I don’t think all of us have been together for a while,” Jeter said, “so it will be nice to see them all together.”

MOSCOW — Russia retaliated on Thursday for Western sanctions against Moscow, announcing that it was banning imports of a wide range of food and agricultural products from Europe and the United States, among others. The move raised the level of confrontation over Ukraine with measures that seemed likely to affect Russian consumers at least as much as European farming.
Dmitri A. Medvedev, the prime minister, announced that Russia would ban all beef, pork, fruit, vegetables and dairy products from the European Union, the United States, Canada, Australia and Norway for one year.
“We hoped until the very last that our foreign colleagues would realize that sanctions are a dead end and that nobody needs them,” Mr. Medvedev said. “Things have turned out in such a way that we have to implement retaliatory measures.”
Russia was still considering various measures involving aviation, including a ban on flights over Siberia, which would affect routes used by European and American airlines that fly to Asia, he told a cabinet meeting broadcast live on state-run satellite news channels.
But while Russians rich enough to savor fine European food at home may lament, at least in private, the gradual disappearance of such fare from shelves after Thursday’s announcement, Europe’s farmers and food producers, at least initially, suggested the effect of the ban was most likely to be limited.
The president of the European Central Bank, Mario Draghi, indicated that the greatest impact to Europe might be the atmosphere of uncertainty that the tensions over Ukraine have generated. “Our risks to the recovery were on the downside to begin with, and certainly one of these risks will be the geopolitical developments,” he said at a news conference in Berlin on Thursday. “The recovery remains weak, fragile and uneven.”
After the United States, Russia is the biggest market for European agricultural exports, worth about 11.8 billion euros last year, or roughly $15.7 billion, according to Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics agency. That is about 10 percent of European agricultural trade; the vast majority of that commerce stays within the 28-nation bloc.
In the past two years, myriad bans imposed by Russia — usually citing health and hygiene problems with European and North American products — have already driven food trade with Russia from peak levels. German pork exports, for instance, totaled 83,000 tons in the first four months of 2013, but fell “drastically,” to just 9,000 tons over the same period this year, the German Farmers’ Association said.
A blanket ban on European pork imports last February has driven prices in Russia “significantly higher,” the association added in a statement, meaning that the Russian consumer is bearing the brunt of the move.
Economic analysts suggested that the additional measures announced by Moscow on Thursday could have an immediate but moderate impact on the Russian economy while the country seeks alternative suppliers in Latin America, Africa and Turkey.
Continue reading the main story
“Even if Russia says it will try to find additional sources of supply, it will be difficult in the short term,” said Ivan Tchakarov, the chief economist at Citibank for Russia. “Consumers will feel some pinch but I don’t think it will be a massive impact.”
“The key question is what the effect on inflation will be,” he added. The bank is estimating that price increases could add one or two points to the inflation rate for 2014, currently running around 6.5 percent.
In announcing the likely ban on Wednesday, President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia seemed keenly aware of the danger of price rises, saying that they should be avoided if possible. But no matter the fallout on the urban, Brie-eating elite — who don’t like Mr. Putin much anyway — the Kremlin move was viewed as another way for the president to enhance his already substantial support base.
In an opinion poll conducted Aug. 1 to 4 by the Levada Center, Mr. Putin’s approval rating hit 87 percent, having risen steadily since the annexation of Crimea last March. The last boost in support appears to be fueled by his confrontation with the West, with the idea that he is restoring Russia to its rightful place in the world.
Analysts considered the choice of food and agriculture products an obvious one after Western nations imposed three rounds of sanctions and ordinary Russians were waiting to hear what the Kremlin’s response would be.
“The consensus of 80 percent of Russians is that we have to reply, that we will fight,” said Igor Yurgens, the economist who runs the Institute of Contemporary Development, noting it was part of a patriotic wave rolling over the country.
In addition, people living in rural areas who make their living from agriculture or food processing or some related industry make up about 30 percent of Russia’s population, he said. They are an important support base for Mr. Putin and have been pushing the substitution of local products for imported ones.
Giant supermarket chains and restaurants scrambled to line up new supplies, and consumers dependent on goods like lactose-free milk imported from Finland worried about whether it could be produced locally. Some products, including baby food and wine, were purposely left out of the ban.
But nationalist Russian leaders crowed that another victory over Western products was at hand.
“We should have started to protect the market much earlier,” said Gennadi Zuganov, the head of the Communist Party, now part of the loyal opposition. “We have everything we need to make it.”
Western experts read Thursday’s blanket ban as an alarming signal that hard-liners close to Mr. Putin were gaining influence.
“It is a complete mystery to me what Putin is thinking with this move,” said Wolfram Schrettl, professor of economics at the Free University in Berlin and an expert on Russia and Eastern Europe. “It is an own goal,” he said, using the soccer term for when a team scores for its opponent by putting the ball in its own net. “Western agriculture can certainly bear the effects.”

In Russia, he predicted, “it will look soon like the Soviet Safeway — empty shelves.” Brazil, for instance, may be ready to increase deliveries of chicken to make up for the absence of such supplies from the United States. “But it is awkward, and requires extreme efforts.”
In Europe, the effect may be the opposite. Albert Jan Maat, chairman of the Dutch Federation of Agriculture and Horticulture, warned that the Russian ban could spur a glut of farm products in Europe, causing prices to drop. “We’re thinking of either removing products from the market or temporarily storing them,” he said.
In other quarters, the Russian ban was met less with alarm than derision. In Poland, after Russia announced its first ban on some fruit and vegetable imports last week, a campaign for Poles to “eat apples” and “drink cider,” drew an immediate and immense response with journalists, celebrities and even President Bronislaw Komorowski signing up and posting selfies eating apples on social media.
Apple eating aside, reactions in Poland to Russia’s retaliatory actions have been increasingly critical. “All of this might be just a part of Putin’s game,” agriculture minister Marek Sawicki, told reporters. “He will try to divide Europe.”
Mr. Sawicki confirmed that Poland would seek compensation in Brussels, as might Finland and perhaps the Baltic nations, where ports, for instance, might suffer as a result of the ban.
Any such compensation would likely come as emergency payments from the vast well of joint European Union funding known as the Common Agricultural Policy. But Frédéric Vincent, a spokesman for the European Commission, said it was “way too early” to make such payments.
The most noticeable American food import to Russia is chicken. But even there,
Russian currently accounts
for just 7 percent of United States poultry export volume, compared with 40 percent of the total in the mid-1990s, according to the National Chicken Council. But the council said the sanctions would not have much of an impact. “As its domestic poultry industry has expanded, Russia has in recent years become less important as an export market,” the council said in a statement.
Echoing the German farm association, it added, “The biggest impact, we believe, will be on Russian citizens who will be burdened by higher prices for all food products, especially meat and poultry.”
Correction: August 7, 2014
Because of an editing error, an earlier version of this article misidentified the source for the statement that Russia accounted for 7 percent of United States poultry export volumes, compared with 40 percent of the total in the mid 1990s. It was the National Chicken Council, not the International Trade Center.

The actress talks to Eric Spitznagel about reforming her deadpan ways and longing for simpler times in Hollywood.
Your latest film, “About Alex,” has been called “ ‘The Big Chill’ for millennials.” Is there a way to describe it that doesn’t sound like a terrible studio pitch?
I’m the worst at describing anything. I can barely put sentences together. It’s about a bunch of friends who go in the woods and some of them have sex with each other and some of them fight and they learn things and you realize that the only thing that matters is love and the connections we have and that the Internet is evil.
Your character in “About Alex” is not at all like April Ludgate, your character from “Parks and Recreation.” Is it a challenge to play someone who isn’t droll or deadpan, or is it a relief to finally get away from that?
It’s a fun challenge to make people accept me as not April and to show that I can do more than roll my eyes. But everything is a challenge for me. Waking up is challenging for me. I can barely put my clothes on in the morning.
You’re so sarcastic that it’s sometimes difficult to tell when you’re being sincere.
Believe me, it’s a bigger problem for me. I don’t even know when I’m being serious or not. I can’t tell how I truly feel about anything.
Can your friends or family tell when you’re being genuine with them?
Sometimes. I think it’s just the tone of my voice that throws people off. Zooey Deschanel recently told me, “Everything that you say to someone sounds like you’re mocking them.” I was like, “But I’m not.” And she was like, “Even when you just said that, it sounded like you were mocking me.”
You have another movie coming out this month, “Life After Beth,” in which you play a zombie. Did you watch a lot of classic zombie movies to prepare for that?
I decided to purposely not watch anything and just kind of wing it. Because I have this brewing demonic monstrous energy inside of me, and I’ve never really had a way to express it. So I didn’t prepare at all. I just went with my instincts. I was like, I’m just going to see what happens when I tap into my monster self.
I doubt many people think, Aubrey Plaza, yeah, she’s got a real rage inside her. That’s a bit surprising.
I’m holding a lot of things in. Let’s just leave it at that. Every movie that I do is cathartic, because in my real life I do have a problem with, you know, emoting and letting my feelings out.
The movie also stars your B.F.F., Anna Kendrick. Is it fair to describe her as your B.F.F.?
For your purposes, yes. Why not?
You’ve gone on a trip to Mexico with her. You were her Oscars date. You tweet to each other adorably. It seems only a matter of time before you get matching tattoos.
It’s true. We have a very deep connection, and it’s hard to have friendships in this town. We have a mutual respect for each other, professionally and personally. And we’re also sexually attracted to each other. That’s another kind of layer of our relationship. We always talk about how we were born in the wrong era of Hollywood. I feel like we could have really ruled the 1930s MGM studio system. If we’d been signed with MGM, we would have owned that [expletive]. But it’s not really like that anymore.
Why does the old Hollywood studio system seem so appealing to you?
There’s just something kind of old-school about being signed with a bunch of other actresses and having to hustle and compete in that way. Now any old person can just, you know, pop up out of nowhere.
I thought you were going to say YouTube and the kids.
Well, I was going to say that. Still, I want Mr. Meyer to, like, call me up to his office and tell me that I’ve got a four-picture deal. That’s what I want, but that’s not going to happen. Instead, I’ve got to do sexy photo shoots, and I don’t even know what I’m doing.
You don’t like the promotional part of it, the photo shoots and interviews and talk shows?
Have you ever seen me on a talk show? I’m the worst interview guest ever.

The music world has been graced by many a pop diva. Whitney Houston, Madonna, Aretha Franklin, Mariah Carey, Jennifer Lopez, Diana Ross, Barbra Streisand and Lady Gaga have all reigned the stage at some point. Is Beyoncé queen now?
Who is your favorite pop diva?
Jody Rosen writes about Beyoncé’s pop-stardom in the T Magazine feature article
“The Woman on Top of the World.”
If you’ve ever seen Beyoncé Knowles astride a concert stage or a red carpet, you know she is a woman with a flair for dramatic entrances. But no previous coup de théâtre prepared the world for the arrival of the singer’s fifth full-length solo record, “Beyoncé,” the “visual album” that airdropped onto iTunes at midnight on Dec. 13, 2013. For months, the music press had seethed with speculation about Beyoncé’s delayed record release, with rumors of disastrous studio sessions and dozens of scrapped songs. “There is utter disarray in Beyoncé’s camp,” the website MediaTakeOut.com hissed. It was an unheard-of turn of events for Beyoncé, whose career had been a testament to, as it were, array: a regal, orderly parade from hit to hit, milestone to milestone, strength to strength.
Sure enough, the alleged behind-the-scenes chaos turned out to be the usual behind-the-scenes order, in disguise: While the gossip mills whirred, Beyoncé stealthily recorded 14 songs and shot 17 videos, which she unleashed in that December sneak attack. Purely as a feat of information management, “Beyoncé” was impressive. The National Security Agency couldn’t stop its secrets from spilling all over the place; Beyoncé kept the lid on a project which, conservatively, involved hundreds of individuals — studio musicians, cameramen, key grips, personal assistants, even record executives, as a rule the least trustworthy people on the planet. The arrival of all that music, all at once and out of the blue, was an unprecedented shock-and-awe move, which rocked the record industry back on its heels and convulsed the Internet. A single Beyoncé video is capable of staggering the senses; the simultaneous release of 17 of them — an onslaught of sound and spectacle and costumes and choreography and, in the case of a video like the one for “Rocket,” stately slow-motion images of billowing silk sheets and water droplets tumbling onto Beyoncé’s bare midriff — it was a lot to process. We can only imagine the feelings of Beyoncé’s pop diva competitors, whose carefully plotted monthslong album rollouts were instantly rendered quaint, and moot. That whining, whirring sound you heard on Dec. 13, mingling with the strains of “Drunk in Love” — that was Lady Gaga, in her gloomy castle keep, chainsawing a meat dress into sackcloth.

The story of
Lizzie Borden
— tried and acquitted, yet still often assumed guilty in the 1892 ax murder of her father and stepmother — was a tantalizing spur to artists, inspiring Agnes de Mille’s 1948 ballet, “Fall River Legend,” and Jack Beeson’s 1965 opera, “Lizzie Borden.” While Beeson, who died in 2010, and his librettist, Kenward Elmslie, created a memorably anxious, creepy work, its three acts all but ensured it would remain a rarity.
But last year, Boston Lyric Opera presented the premiere of a chamber version, condensed to a single act by Todd Bashore and John Conklin, which may give the piece a new lease on life. That production, staged by Christopher Alden and conducted by David Angus, travels to Tanglewood on Thursday with the Boston cast, including the mezzo-soprano Heather Johnson in the title role and the soprano Caroline Worra and the bass-baritone Daniel Mobbs as her repressive, doomed parents. (8 p.m., Ozawa Hall, Lenox, Mass., 888-266-1200,

.)
